Chapter 4: Taking Responsibility—Choosing Growth Over Blame
As the meantime unfolds, something subtle but powerful starts to shift. You might notice that urge to blame others—for heartbreak, disappointment, or even loneliness—slowly losing its grip. In its place, a new sense of responsibility begins to take root. And here’s the thing: this isn’t about taking on all the fault. It’s about recognizing that you have the power to shape your own life. Let me tell you about a woman who, for years, found herself caught in a cycle of unfulfilling relationships. She’d point fingers at her partners—maybe they were too distant, too needy, or just unreliable. But in the quiet of her meantime, she noticed a pattern. She was the one common thread. That realization stung, but it also brought a kind of relief. If she was part of the problem, then she could also be part of the solution. You know, most of us resist this kind of self-examination. It’s so much easier to believe that our happiness depends on what someone else does—or doesn’t do. But the meantime doesn’t let us off the hook that easily. It gently asks, “What choices have I made? What beliefs have I been holding onto? How have I played a part in my own pain?” These questions aren’t here to shame you. They’re here to give you power. Because when you start taking responsibility for your own growth, you reclaim your ability to change. Take the story of a man who, after a painful breakup, realized he’d been ignoring red flags right from the start. He wanted the relationship to work so badly that he overlooked his own needs and boundaries. But in the meantime, he began practicing honesty—with himself, and with others. He learned to speak up when something didn’t feel right, even if it meant risking a bit of conflict. The more he honored his own truth, the less he felt like a victim of circumstance. Taking responsibility also means letting go of the urge to control others. So many of us fall into the habit of trying to fix, change, or even rescue those we care about. But the meantime has a way of teaching us that real growth only comes from within. You can’t force someone else to heal, or to love you differently. The only person you can truly change—is yourself. Sure, this shift can feel uncomfortable. It takes humility, courage, and a willingness to face some tough truths. But here’s the freedom: when you stop blaming and start taking responsibility, the past stops dictating your future. Suddenly, new choices open up—and so does the path to love and fulfillment. Spiritual practice can really help here. Some people find strength by surrendering to a higher power, trusting that growth is happening in its own time. Others lean on community, mentors, or simple rituals that remind them of their own agency. The meantime becomes your training ground for self-awareness, resilience, and hope. As you start to take responsibility, your relationships shift too. Old patterns of conflict, resentment, or codependency begin to give way to something healthier. There’s a new sense of clarity about what you need, what’s possible, and what’s truly worth letting go. So, the meantime—once seen as a burden—becomes a real gift. It’s your chance to become the person who’s truly ready for real love.
